screens.title: Asset Bundles & Addressables
screens.subtitle: Deliver, update, and manage game content dynamically

narration.text: As your Unity projects grow, packaging every texture, model, and audio file into the initial build quickly bloats download size and complicates updates. In this lesson you will learn the practical purpose of Asset Bundles and why the Addressables system is the recommended way to manage them. Asset Bundles let you store platform-specific assets separately and load them at runtime, enabling streaming of optional content, smaller initial downloads, and incremental updates. Addressables builds on top of bundles to give you a name-based A P I, automatic dependency handling, and a generated catalog that maps addresses to physical locations. We will cover the full flow: marking assets as Addressable, organizing groups, building bundles, loading assets at runtime with AsyncOperationHandle, and correctly releasing resources to avoid memory leaks. You will also see a simple loader script pattern and a hands-on activity to try in the Editor. By the end you will understand when to use bundles, how Addressables simplifies deployment, and what common mistakes to avoid when loading and unloading assets.

narration.text: These objectives map to practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you will understand why Asset Bundles exist: they separate optional and platform-specific content from your main build so you can stream or download assets later. A concrete example is shipping a core game and downloading extra levels as bundles only when requested. Second, you will configure and build bundles and groups for different platforms and learn how the Addressables build generates a catalog that maps addresses to physical locations. Third, you will implement runtime loading patterns using Addressables APIs, see how AsyncOperationHandle represents asynchronous work, and practice instantiating prefabs and applying textures and audio. Fourth, you will manage dependencies, memory, and versioning by explicitly releasing handles and using the catalog to deploy updated bundles. Each objective includes how it is verified: build a small lab that marks three assets as Addressable, loads and unloads them, and confirms memory returns to baseline in the Profiler. These outcomes reduce build size and make updates safer.

screens.title: What is an Asset Bundle?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and an everyday example

narration.text: An Asset Bundle is a platform-specific archive that contains assets and their dependencies for runtime loading. Think of it as a compressed package you can download or stream later instead of shipping every file with the initial build. The practical benefit is obvious: if you have optional levels, seasonal skins, or language packs, you can keep them out of the main build and retrieve them when the player requests them. For example, ship the core game with base characters and download a new seasonal skin bundle when a player selects it. Asset Bundles carry platform variations, so you build a bundle for Android and another optimized bundle for iOS if their texture compression differs. A common misconception is that bundles magically manage memory; they only provide packaging and delivery. Loading a bundled asset still consumes memory and must be released by your code or the higher-level system you choose. Key takeaway: bundles solve delivery and update problems, but you still manage loading, unloading, and platform differences. What is an Asset Bundle? means a deployable archive of platform-specific assets used for runtime dynamic delivery and incremental updates.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and an everyday example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Building Asset Bundles and Addressables
screens.subtitle: Editor steps to produce bundles and the catalog

narration.text: Building Asset Bundles and Addressables is a sequence of editor steps that end with deployable bundles and a catalog the runtime can query. Begin by installing Addressables from the Package Manager and creating Addressables Settings if prompted. Next, add assets to Addressables Groups by selecting an asset and checking the Addressable box or dragging it into a group. Each group can have its own settings for compression, build path, and remote hosting. When you are ready, choose Build > New Build > Default Build Script from the Addressables Groups window. Unity will process groups, create platform-specific Asset Bundles, and generate a catalog that maps addresses to bundle locations. A concrete example: create a group for 'SeasonalSkins' set to remote build path; after building, upload the generated bundles to your CDN and host the catalog at a discoverable URL. A common mistake is forgetting to set the correct build target or remote paths, which leads to incompatible bundles or an incorrect catalog. Takeaway: follow a disciplined build flow and verify the generated output before integrating remote hosting. Building Asset Bundles and Addressables means install addressables, group assets, set build paths, run default build script, then deploy bundles and the catalog to appropriate hosts.. screens.title: AddressablesLoader: example script
screens.subtitle: Key API patterns: AssetReference, InstantiateAsync, LoadAssetAsync, and Release

narration.text: This walkthrough presents the AddressablesLoader pattern and explains why each step matters. The script exposes AssetReference fields in the Inspector so designers can assign assets without hard-coded paths. At runtime, InstantiateAsync creates a GameObject instance from an AssetReference and returns a Task you can await. LoadAssetAsync returns an AsyncOperationHandle that you should await to get the asset result for textures or audio. After using loaded assets you must call Addressables. Release(handle) to free memory or Addressables. ReleaseInstance for instantiated GameObjects. A concrete example: you await characterPrefabReference. InstantiateAsync to instantiate the player, then call Addressables. ReleaseInstance when the character should be removed. A frequent misconception is relying on garbage collection alone; Unity's asset memory is separate and requires explicit release calls. Takeaway: use AssetReference for inspector wiring, await Async operations, and release what you load to prevent memory leaks. AddressablesLoader: example script means use assetreference for safe inspector linking, await asyncoperationhandles, and always release handles and instances when finished.. In practical terms, key api patterns: assetreference, instantiateasync, loadassetasync, and release. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › AddressablesLoader
Example Loader
Inspector-friendly fields and explicit release logic make this pattern robust.
// Inspector fields use AssetReference types for safe linking
public AssetReferenceGameObject characterPrefabReference;
public AssetReferenceTexture2D backgroundTextureReference;
public AssetReferenceAudioClip musicClipReference;

public async void LoadAllAssets() {
    // Instantiate prefab using AssetReference
    var character = await characterPrefabReference.InstantiateAsync().Task;
    // Load a texture via Addressables.LoadAssetAsync
    var texHandle = Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<Texture2D>(backgroundTextureReference);
    await texHandle.Task;
    // Remember to release handles and instances when done
    Addressables.Release(texHandle);
}

public void UnloadAllAssets() {
    Addressables.ReleaseInstance(character);
    // Release other handles similarly
}
What to watch for
Await Tasks from InstantiateAsync and LoadAssetAsync, store handles to release later, and avoid assuming GC will free asset memory.
Misconception
Instantiating a prefab does not imply automatic release; you must call ReleaseInstance explicitly to free related memory.
Key Takeaway

AssetReference + explicit release = predictable memory lifecycle for runtime-loaded content.

screens.title: Addressables architecture and the catalog
screens.subtitle: How addresses, groups, bundles, and the catalog fit together

narration.text: Addressables sits on top of Asset Bundles and direct loading to provide a single name-based A P I. The core pieces are AssetReference or address strings, Addressables Groups, the generated Asset Bundles, and the catalog. When you build, Unity processes groups into bundles and emits a catalog file that maps an address to the bundle or local path. At runtime, the Addressables system reads the catalog and resolves addresses to physical locations so your code calls Addressables. LoadAssetAsync with a simple name and the system finds the right bundle or direct source. The catalog enables remote updates: by replacing the catalog on your server you can repoint addresses to new bundles without patching the main application. A misconception is thinking Addressables hides all platform differences; it simplifies them but you still set group-level build settings for platform-specific compression. Takeaway: the catalog is the indirection layer that decouples code from where assets live, enabling safer refactoring and remote deployment. Addressables architecture and the catalog means the catalog maps addresses to physical bundle locations and enables runtime resolution and remote updates without rebuilding the player.. In practical terms, how addresses, groups, bundles, and the catalog fit together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Addressables architecture
Components
Addresses, Groups, Bundles, and Catalog are the primary parts to understand.
Address / AssetReference
A stable name you use to request an asset at runtime.
Addressables Group
Organizes assets for packing, compression, and remote settings.
Asset Bundles
Generated archives for each platform containing the grouped assets.
Catalog
A lookup table that maps addresses to the bundle or local path the runtime should load.
Runtime resolution
At runtime, Addressables consults the catalog to resolve an address to its physical bundle or file. This allows your code to remain unchanged when you move assets between bundles or hosts.
Misconception
Addressables replaces platform configuration. It simplifies resolution but you still set platform-specific build settings in groups for correct compression and compatibility.
Key Takeaway

The catalog is the indirection that decouples code from storage location, enabling remote updates and safer refactoring.

screens.title: Marking and grouping Addressable assets
screens.subtitle: Editor practices that keep projects manageable

narration.text: Marking assets as Addressable and organizing them into groups is a small but crucial authoring activity. The simplest way is to select an asset in the Project window and check the Addressable checkbox in the Inspector or drag the asset into an Addressables Group. Prefer meaningful addresses rather than auto-generated paths to make runtime requests clearer. Create groups by content type or by deployment strategy: for example, a 'LocalCore' group for essential assets built into the player and a 'RemoteDLC' group for optional downloadable content. Set group-level build and load paths: local groups will pack inside the player, remote groups will output bundles to a remote build path and require you to host them. A common pitfall is scattering addresses with inconsistent naming; that increases the chance of runtime lookup errors. Takeaway: adopt a consistent grouping and naming convention that matches your deployment and update plans so teams can reliably reference assets and update content without breaking runtime loads. Marking and grouping Addressable assets means group assets by deployment strategy and use stable, readable addresses to keep runtime lookup predictable and team-friendly.. screens.title: Asset Bundles vs Addressables
screens.subtitle: When to manage bundles directly and when to prefer Addressables

narration.text: Asset Bundles and Addressables are not competing technologies; Addressables is a high-level system built on top of Asset Bundles and direct asset loading. Use direct Asset Bundles if you need a low-level, custom packaging pipeline or have unique runtime constraints that require explicit bundle management. However, Addressables is recommended in most cases because it provides name-based loading, automatic dependency tracking, and a generated catalog that decouples code from storage. A concrete contrast: if you manually create bundles you must implement your own mapping layer and dependency tracking. Addressables does that work for you and exposes a simpler A P I like LoadAssetAsync and AssetReference. InstantiateAsync. A common misconception is that Addressables adds runtime overhead that makes it unsuitable for performance-sensitive code. In practice, Addressables is optimized for typical use and gives you control over grouping and compression to tune performance. Takeaway: prefer Addressables for maintainability and safer runtime resolution unless you have specific reasons to manage bundles directly. Asset Bundles vs Addressables means addressables simplifies loading and dependency management and is the recommended modern approach unless you need a bespoke bundle pipeline.. In practical terms, when to manage bundles directly and when to prefer addressables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: AsyncOperationHandle and runtime patterns
screens.subtitle: Awaiting handles, checking status, and applying results

narration.text: AsyncOperationHandle represents an asynchronous load operation and is central to runtime Addressables patterns. When you call LoadAssetAsync you receive a handle that contains status and, on success, the requested asset. Await the handle's Task to pause code until completion or register a completion callback if you prefer event-style control. Always check the handle's Status to confirm success and inspect OperationException on failure. For example, after awaiting a texture handle, assign the returned texture to a RawImage component. A common mistake is discarding handles immediately; keep a reference to each handle you plan to release later. When instantiating GameObjects, prefer AssetReference. InstantiateAsync which returns a Task for the instantiated object and can be released with ReleaseInstance. Takeaway: await handles, check status, store handles for release, and always handle failure paths to avoid silent runtime errors. AsyncOperationHandle and runtime patterns means await or observe asyncoperationhandles, validate success, use results, and store handles so you can release them later to free memory.. In practical terms, awaiting handles, checking status, and applying results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Handle lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Await or observe AsyncOperationHandles, validate success, use results, and store handles so you can Release them later to free memory.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › AsyncOperationHandle
Pattern: load, check, use, release
A robust runtime loader always checks handle status and releases handles when finished.
// Load and await
var handle = Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<Texture2D>(address);
await handle.Task;
if (handle.Status == AsyncOperationStatus.Succeeded) {
    var tex = handle.Result;
    // Apply texture to UI or material
}
// Later, release to free memory
Addressables.Release(handle);
Failure handling
If the handle fails, check OperationException for details and provide user feedback such as retry or fallback content.
Key Takeaway

Keep handles alive while using results, inspect status after awaiting, and always release to prevent leaks.

screens.title: Memory management and Release patterns
screens.subtitle: How to avoid leaks and why Release calls are essential

narration.text: Memory management with Addressables is explicit: when you load an asset it consumes memory and will not be freed until you call the appropriate Release method. For assets loaded via LoadAssetAsync use Addressables. Release(handle), passing the AsyncOperationHandle you received. For GameObjects created with InstantiateAsync, call Addressables. ReleaseInstance to ensure the instance and its referenced assets are freed. A concrete pattern: store handles in fields when you load assets, and in your scene cleanup call Release or ReleaseInstance for each stored handle or instance. A common error is relying on scene unloads or garbage collection; both may not free the native memory used by textures or audio. On memory-constrained devices like mobile this mistake leads to steadily increasing memory usage and eventual crashes. To validate correct behavior, use the Profiler before and after release calls to confirm memory returns toward a baseline. Takeaway: track handles, release deterministically, and always verify with profiling tools to avoid runtime leaks. Memory management and Release patterns means store and release handles or instances explicitly. validate memory with the profiler to ensure releases free native memory.. In practical terms, how to avoid leaks and why release calls are essential. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Release deterministically
keyIdea.text: Store and release handles or instances explicitly. Validate memory with the Profiler to ensure releases free native memory.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Memory & Release
Release patterns
Always pair load operations with a corresponding release when the asset or instance is no longer needed.
Load with handle
var handle = Addressables.LoadAssetAsync; store handle; use result; Addressables.Release(handle) when done.
Instantiate
Use AssetReference.InstantiateAsync and call Addressables.ReleaseInstance when destroying the instance.
Profiler verification
Check memory usage before and after release to ensure native memory is freed.
Common error
Assuming scene unloads automatically release Addressables-managed memory. They may not; explicit releases are required.
Key Takeaway

Treat Addressables loads like any native allocation: store references and release them deterministically, and verify with the Profiler.

screens.title: Dependency tracking and catalog versioning
screens.subtitle: How Addressables ensures dependent assets are loaded and how updates work

narration.text: Addressables simplifies dependency management by tracking what assets depend on others and loading those dependencies as needed. For example, a material that references a texture will cause the texture dependency to be included and loaded when the material address is requested. During build, Unity includes dependency information in the bundles and catalog so at runtime Addressables can load both the requested asset and its dependencies automatically. For versioning and updates, the catalog is the single point that maps addresses to bundle locations. To update content remotely, build new bundles and a new catalog, upload them to your server, and ensure clients download the updated catalog. A misconception is thinking updating a bundle file alone is sufficient; if the client's catalog still points to an old bundle name it won't fetch the new content. Takeaway: dependency tracking reduces developer work for complex asset graphs, and correct catalog deployment is essential for remote updates to take effect. Dependency tracking and catalog versioning means addressables loads dependencies automatically and uses the catalog to map updated bundles to addresses for safe remote updates.. In practical terms, how addressables ensures dependent assets are loaded and how updates work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dependency & versioning
keyIdea.text: Addressables loads dependencies automatically and uses the catalog to map updated bundles to addresses for safe remote updates.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Dependency & Catalog
Automatic dependency handling
Addressables ensures that when you request an asset, its dependencies are also available.
How it works
Dependency data is included in the build so the runtime can load all required items in the right order.
Versioning via catalog
Replace the catalog on your server and clients will resolve addresses to new bundle locations after updating the catalog.
Concrete example
A material address triggers the texture dependency to load automatically so you only request the material address in code.
Misconception
Uploading new bundle files without updating the hosted catalog means clients keep referencing old bundle locations and won't fetch updates.

screens.title: Build, deploy, and update timeline
screens.subtitle: A practical timeline for content releases using Addressables

narration.text: When planning content releases with Addressables, treat the process as a timeline: author, group, build, verify, deploy, and monitor. First, author assets and mark them Addressable. Second, organize assets into groups and set build and load paths depending on whether content will be local or remote. Third, run the Default Build Script to generate bundles and the catalog. Fourth, verify the build locally by loading the new catalog in a staging build and testing loads, instantiation, and releases. Fifth, deploy by uploading bundles and the catalog to your hosting server. Finally, monitor runtime usage and Profiler traces post-deployment to detect unexpected memory growth. A common mistake is skipping staged verification and directly deploying to production. Takeaway: a staged build and verification step prevents broken mappings or platform mismatches from reaching players, and the catalog is the critical file that you must update on the host for clients to discover new bundles. Build, deploy, and update timeline means author → group → build → verify in staging → deploy bundles and catalog → monitor profiler for correct memory behavior.. In practical terms, a practical timeline for content releases using addressables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Build & Deploy Timeline
Timeline steps
A repeatable sequence for safe content delivery.
1. Author & mark
Create assets and mark Addressable with meaningful addresses.
2. Group & configure
Set local vs remote paths and compression per group.
3. Build & verify
Run Default Build Script and test loads in a staging client.
4. Deploy catalog + bundles
Upload generated files to your host and ensure the catalog is accessible.
5. Monitor & profile
Use the Profiler to confirm assets are released and memory stabilizes after updates.
Pitfall to avoid
Deploying bundles without updating the hosted catalog or verifying the build target will break runtime resolution on clients.

narration.text: Keep three ideas at the front of your mind. First, Asset Bundle: a platform-specific archive used to deliver assets at runtime so you can reduce initial build size and stream content. Second, Addressables System: the recommended, high-level layer that uses addresses and a catalog to load assets and their dependencies robustly, simplifying refactors and remote updates. Third, Release A P I: Addressables. Release and Addressables. ReleaseInstance are essential tools to free memory after loading or instantiating assets; forgetting them is the most common cause of leaks. These three concepts—packaging, resolution, and deterministic release—work together to let you deliver rich content without sacrificing performance or maintainability. As you practice in the lab, focus on consistent naming, correct build targets, and validating memory behavior with the Profiler. Which of these three will be the first one you verify in your project?

keyIdea.title: Three quick reminders
keyIdea.text: Bundle for delivery, Addressables for resolution, Release for memory safety.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three compact cards to recall the most important ideas.
Asset Bundle
An archive of platform-specific assets prepared for runtime delivery.
Addressables
A name-based system with automatic dependency handling and a runtime catalog.
Release APIs
Addressables.Release and ReleaseInstance must be called to free loaded asset memory.
Summary

Use bundles to deliver content, Addressables to resolve it by address and manage dependencies, and explicit release calls to keep memory under control.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three actionable reminders before you start the lab

narration.text: Before you open the Editor, remember these actionable items. First, install Addressables from the Package Manager and create Addressables Settings so groups exist. Second, mark three test assets as Addressable: a prefab, a background texture, and an audio clip. Use short, stable addresses for each so you can load them by name in code. Third, after building and loading assets in your test scene, store their AsyncOperationHandles and call Addressables. Release or Addressables. ReleaseInstance when those assets are no longer needed. A short verification flow: run the scene, open the Profiler, press load to instantiate the prefab and observe memory increase, then call unload and confirm memory decreases. This quick checklist will make your lab productive and help you avoid the most common pitfalls related to unresolved addresses, wrong build targets, and unreleased assets.

keyIdea.title: Pre-lab checklist
keyIdea.text: Install, mark three assets, use stable addresses, build, test loads, and always release handles after use.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Quick Reference
Quick Reference
Three last-minute reminders before the hands-on lab.
Install
Open Package Manager, install Addressables, and create Addressables Settings.
Mark Assets
Select a prefab, texture, and audio, check Addressable or drag to a Group, and set clear addresses.
Test & Release
Build Addressables, run the scene, store handles, and call Release or ReleaseInstance when done.
Final Tip

Always verify build target and catalog mapping in staging before rolling updates to players.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute interactive lab walkthrough video. Start by installing the Addressables package. Then, demonstrate how to mark assets (prefab, texture, audio) as Addressable and organize them into groups in the Addressables Groups window. Walk through the process of building Addressables content. Next, live-code the `AddressablesLoader` script, explaining `AssetReference`, `LoadAssetAsync`, `InstantiateAsync`, and crucially, `Release` and `ReleaseInstance`. Show the game running, loading, and unloading assets, with the Unity Profiler open to visualize memory usage before and after releasing assets. Include a mini-quiz asking about the importance of `Release()` methods.
